title: Game Development
summary: Real-time interactive simulation. The threshold is the frame budget: everything (input, physics, AI, rendering) must fit in about 16 ms, sixty times a second, and the game must behave the same at any frame rate.

nodes.label: The Game Loop
nodes.summary: Process input, update the world, render; repeat as fast as the frame budget allows.
nodes.outcome: Write a game loop and name its three phases.
nodes.check: What are the three phases of a classic game loop?
nodes.answer: Process input, update the game state, render.

nodes.label: Frame Budget & Delta Time
nodes.summary: At 60 fps each frame has about 16.7 ms. Movement scaled by elapsed time (delta time) keeps the game speed independent of frame rate.
nodes.outcome: Make movement frame-rate independent with delta time.
nodes.check: How many milliseconds does one frame have at 60 fps?

nodes.label: "Move a fixed amount every frame"
nodes.summary: Per-frame movement makes the game run faster on fast machines and slower on slow ones.
nodes.check: A character moves 5 pixels per frame. What happens on a 144 Hz monitor compared with 60 Hz?
nodes.answer: It moves 2.4 times faster; movement must be scaled by delta time.

nodes.label: Fixed Timestep Physics
nodes.summary: Run physics in fixed steps with an accumulator and interpolate rendering, for stable and deterministic simulation.
nodes.outcome: Implement an accumulator loop with a fixed physics step.
nodes.check: Why run physics at a fixed timestep instead of the variable frame time?
nodes.answer: Variable steps make integration unstable and results differ between machines; fixed steps are stable and deterministic.

nodes.label: Vectors & Transforms
nodes.summary: Positions, directions, dot and cross products, and matrices for translate, rotate and scale.
nodes.outcome: Use a dot product to decide whether an enemy is in front of the player.
nodes.check: The dot product of the player's facing direction and the direction to an enemy is negative. Where is the enemy?
nodes.answer: Behind the player (more than 90° away from the facing direction).

nodes.label: Collision Detection
nodes.summary: Bounding volumes, broad phase and narrow phase; fast objects can tunnel through thin walls.
nodes.outcome: Write an AABB overlap test and explain tunnelling.
nodes.check: Why can a fast bullet pass through a thin wall without colliding?
nodes.answer: Tunnelling: between two frames it jumps from one side to the other, so no frame sees an overlap.

nodes.label: The Rendering Pipeline
nodes.summary: Vertices transformed to the screen, rasterised to fragments, shaded and depth-tested on the GPU.
nodes.outcome: Trace a triangle through vertex shading, rasterisation and fragment shading.
nodes.check: What does the depth buffer (z-buffer) decide?
nodes.answer: Which surface is nearest the camera at each pixel, so hidden surfaces are not drawn over visible ones.

nodes.label: Shaders
nodes.summary: Small programs run in parallel on the GPU for every vertex or pixel.
nodes.outcome: Write a fragment shader that tints by distance.
nodes.check: Why are shaders fast at per-pixel work?
nodes.answer: The GPU runs the same small program on thousands of pixels in parallel.

nodes.label: Entity-Component-System
nodes.summary: Entities are IDs, components are plain data, systems process all entities with a set of components: composition over inheritance and cache-friendly memory.
nodes.outcome: Model a game object with components instead of an inheritance tree.
nodes.check: What problem with deep inheritance does ECS avoid?
nodes.answer: Rigid hierarchies where a new combination of behaviours (e.g. a flying, swimming enemy) does not fit any branch.

nodes.label: Pathfinding (A*)
nodes.summary: Search a graph using cost so far plus an admissible heuristic to find shortest paths efficiently.
nodes.outcome: Run A* on a grid and explain the role of the heuristic.
nodes.check: What must be true of A*'s heuristic for it to guarantee the shortest path?
nodes.answer: It must be admissible: it never overestimates the true remaining cost.

nodes.label: "Always step toward the goal"
nodes.summary: Greedy movement gets stuck behind obstacles; search must sometimes move away from the goal to reach it.
nodes.outcome: Show a map where greedy movement fails and A* succeeds.
nodes.check: An enemy always moves to the tile closest to the player. What happens at a U-shaped wall between them?
nodes.answer: It gets stuck inside the U, because escaping requires moving away from the player first.

nodes.label: Game AI: State Machines & Behaviour Trees
nodes.summary: Readable, designer-tunable decision logic for characters.
nodes.outcome: Build a guard's patrol–chase–search behaviour as a state machine.
nodes.check: Why do game studios often prefer behaviour trees to large state machines?
nodes.answer: They scale better: behaviours are modular and reusable without an explosion of transitions.

nodes.label: Multiplayer Netcode
nodes.summary: Latency hidden with client-side prediction, server reconciliation and lag compensation; the server stays authoritative.
nodes.outcome: Explain client prediction and reconciliation for a moving player.
nodes.check: Why does the server, not the client, decide what really happened in a competitive game?
nodes.answer: Clients can be modified to cheat; an authoritative server validates every action.

nodes.label: Profiling & Optimisation
nodes.summary: Measure where the frame time goes before optimising; CPU-bound and GPU-bound frames need different fixes.
nodes.outcome: Use a profiler to find whether a frame is CPU- or GPU-bound.
nodes.check: Lowering the resolution doesn't raise your frame rate. What does that suggest?
nodes.answer: The game is CPU-bound, not GPU-bound.

nodes.label: Game Design & Game Feel
nodes.summary: Core loops, feedback, juice and difficulty curves; playtesting with real players.
nodes.outcome: Define a core loop and run a playtest that changes it.
nodes.check: Why watch playtesters silently instead of explaining the game to them?
nodes.answer: Players won't have you there at release; silent observation reveals where the game itself fails to teach.
